item: PT124-S2-Q11 (Evaluate): garbled chain line
old:
Whenever we're doing Flaw and we see any conditional logic in the premises, we immediately start assuming we'll going to probably see a Necessary vs. Sufficient flaw (where the author supplies a conditional relationship or two in the evidence, but then applies that rule in some backwards or opposite manner to reach the conclusion).
The first sentence has "in order to X, you must Y". The second has "doing A will lead to B".
The conclusion is also a pseudo-conditional, because it's saying "something that is P can be assumed to be Q".
So we might need to diagram these if we're trying to figure out exactly where the author might be making an illegal reversal or negation.
Prem 1: maintain high S.O.L → maintain functioning Inf
Prem 2: major invest in improving Inf → rise in S.O.L
Do those two premises chain together? No, not really. To chain, you need an overlapping term. "Standard of living" is an overlapping term, but we're talking about it in two different ways -- whether or not you're maintaining a **high** standard of living / whether or not your standard of living has risen **higher** than it previously was.
If those were the same we could make this chain: major invest → high S.O.L → maintain in impr Inf. funct. Inf
But they're not. You could raise your standard of living from 150th in the world to 140th. It would be **higher** but it wouldn't be a **high** standard of living that you're maintaining.
Okay, so the conditional premises don't chain together. So is there a conditional logic problem with the conclusion? Yes. The conclusion looks like this: S.O.L is rising → Invested heavily in imp Inf
That's an illegal reversal of the 2nd sentence: invest heavily in imp Inf → rise in S.O.L.
We were told that major investments would lead to a rise in S.O.L.
But other things might also lead to a rise in S.O.L (better daycare and family leave options / cleaner environments / industrial ingenuity creating new jobs and wealth like in Silicon Valley).
If a country's standard of living is on the rise, we can't assume it's because of major infrastructure investment. It might be because of one of these other things that cause standard of living to rise.

item: PT147-S1-Q15 (Evaluate): "Unproven vs. Proven True" should be "Proven False"
old:
Whenever we're doing Flaw and see that the argument has a Rebuttal structure, we want to be sensitive to a few common flaws relating to Rebuttals
  1. Ad Hominem (dismisses a view by saying the source has a biased interest or a conflicting past)
  2. Unproven vs. Proven True (shows that someone failed to prove X but then erroneously concludes from that that X is false)
  3. Straw Man / Irrelevant Response (the rebuttal doesn't seem to have anything to do with falsifying the original position)
  This feels like #3. Why is the author thinking that it's relevant to object by saying, "Success requires a lot of hard work"? Was the popular book saying that "success doesn't require a lot of hard work"? Not as far as we've heard. So in that sense, this author is responding to a position that his opponent doesn't hold (Straw Man) or is rebutting with something irrelevant. When we're doing Flaw and we see conditional logic wording, we know to look out for the #1 famous Necessary vs. Sufficient flaw, in which the author presents a conditional logic relationship and then interprets it in some illegal reversed or negated fashion. We have a couple conditional logic indicator words here: without exception / requires
  The book says:
  successful in business → benefited from luck
  The author's rebuttal is saying:
  successful in business → lots of hard work
  Those don't conflict, of course. Success in business may require luck AND require lots of hard work.

item: PT154-S1-Q9 (Evaluate): confusing "(the only is sufficient)"
old:
We're doing a Flaw question, and we see conditional logic indicators (any, only). What should we be thinking? We should deeply suspect that this is going to commit the #1 Famous Flaw, Necessary vs. Sufficient, which just means that the author presents a conditional logic premise and then botches using it by making an illegal reversal or negation.
The author draws two conclusions, so we should look at each one.
The first (intermediate) conclusion is that there must not be abundant gnats. Why? Because there are no geckos, and geckos are found in every environment with abundant gnats.
```
~Geckos → ~Lots of Gnats
Here = ~Geckos
Thus, Here = ~Lots of Gnats
```
This mini-argument seems airtight. It just applies a fact (no geckos) that triggers the contrapositive of the conditional in the first sentence (lots of gnats → geckos).
Okay the main conclusion was that the climate is not wet.
We were told that gnats survive only in a wet climate. Only / only if are necessary indicators (the only is sufficient), so the idea of "wet climate" goes on the right of the arrow.
```
Gnats → Wet climate
~Wet climate → ~Gnats
```
The author's move from the 2nd to last claim to the final claim is, "If there is not an abundant population of gnats, then it must not be a wet climate." But that move looks like this:
```
~Gnats → ~Wet climate
```
That's not what the rule said. It said "if yes gnats, then yes wet climate", but the author is trying to argue "if no gnats, then no wet climate". That's an illegal negation.

At first we might think, "This doesn't have to be true. Yes, we know that most mail takes 3 or more days, but that doesn't have to be because it's incorrectly addressed. It could be that it's correctly addressed but damaged in transit."

Here's the problem with that -- if we tell ourselves that "most correctly addressed mail is damaged in transit, and thus takes more than 2 days", then we'd be contradicting the first sentence, which says that "nearly all correctly addressed mail arrives within 2 days".

If all mail were correctly addressed, then this paragraph would contradict itself.

If there were 100 pieces of mail, all correctly addressed, we know that nearly all (we'll say 90 of them) get there within 2 days. That leaves 10 pieces of correctly addressed mail not getting there within 2 days.

But we were told that "most pieces of mail" take more than 2 days. 10 is not most of 100. We'd have to keep adding incorrectly addressed mail in order to be able to every honor the idea that most total mail takes more than 2 days.

? pieces of mail 100 correctly addressed ? incorrect 90 arrive w/in 2 days 10 take more than 2 (damaged in transit)

Let's say we added in 50 incorrectly addressed pieces of mail.

150pieces of mail 100 correctly addressed50incorrect 90 arrive w/in 2 days 10 take more than 2 (damaged in transit)

Even if all 50 of those took more than 2 days, and we added in the 10 correctly addressed ones that took more than 2 days, we'd still only be at 60 pieces that took more than 2 days.

And 60 isnotmost of 150. It's less than half. So we'd have to add even more incorrectly addressed pieces of mail.

180pieces of mail 100 correctly addressed80incorrect 90 arrive w/in 2 days 10 take more than 2 (damaged in transit)

Now we could have a total of 90 pieces of mail that took more than 2 days (80 + 10).

90 out of 180 is exactly half, so we'd still need to go a little higher with our incorrectly addressed total to make the "most" fact work.

No matter what number of mail pieces we make the correctly addressed mail, we'll always have the problem that 90% of it gets there within 2 days and only 10% or less takes more than 2 days.

In order to comply with the fact that more than 50% of all mail takes more than 2 days, we need to add a lot of incorrectly addressed mail to make the math work.

If a farmer never bought crop insurance, and this crop failure makes them go bankrupt, the farmer could still be held responsible for that consequence of a wheat crop's failing, for example.

evidence: C: "Farmers are not responsible for the consequences of a wheat crop's failing if wheat growth has been affected by lack of rain."

item: PT145-S4-Q22: breakdown labels sentence 1 "Evidence (for)"; Evaluate template does not match
old: Whenever we do Role and Main Conclusion questions, we expect that 90% of the time the Main Conclusion will appear earlier than at least some of its support. The word "So" attached to the first claim of the 2nd sentence indicates that the 1st sentence is supporting the "So" claim. Thus, the main conclusion can't possibly be the first sentence. The word "for" (FABS: for, after all, because since) indicates support, so we know that the final two claims are there to support the "So" claim that begins the 2nd sentence. Whenever we see a structure like this: X is true. After all, Y is true and thus Z is true. We know that X was the main conclusion, and that the 2nd sentence serves to support X. The "thus" within the 2nd sentence tells us that Y supports Z. Similarly, the "therefore" in the final sentence tells us that "music is merely sound" supports "music by itself creates neither social conditions nor human behavior".

item: PT146-S2-Q26: correct note argues the key reads "backwards" before accepting it
old:
This answer is terribly written, but it wins by the standard of best available. It's certainly similar in sentiment to what we were looking for, "the Nobel rules unfairly exclude some deserving people from getting a Nobel".

But it feels like a backwards version of what we want. This answer sounds like "having a Nobel doesn't mean (doesn't accurately indicate) that you deserved one for your contribution".

However, that's not what they were saying. They were saying, "not getting a Nobel doesn't mean you didn't deserve one for your contribution."

Apparently LSAT was hoping we would hear this answer in a fuzzier way, like, "Whether you have or lack a Nobel is not an accurate indicator of your contributions to science."

But it's pretty obnoxiously sloppy on their part. Again, keep that mantra of "best available" in your head. Occasionally, you may even have to think, "Sigh. This question is technically broken, but what do I think the test writers wanted the credited response to be?"
new:
This answer is abstract, but it matches what we were looking for, "the Nobel rules unfairly exclude some deserving people from getting a Nobel".

Both speakers point to people whose work deserves a prize but who can't get one under the rules: the fourth or fifth scientist behind an important result, or a scientist who died before the work was appreciated.

If deserving contributors can go without a Nobel, then who has a Nobel and who doesn't is not an accurate picture of who contributed what. That's what this answer says. It doesn't require that prizes ever go to undeserving people. Missing deserving people is enough to make Nobel Prizes inaccurate indicators.

"The only" is strong, and thus a red flag, but also conditional, and thus something we should examine by looking at it conditionally (as well as its contrapositive).

"The only" is a sufficient, Left-side indicator word.

So the idea following "the only", a means of making itself unpalatable to predators, would go on the Left of the arrow.

```
a way to make itself      feeding on
highly unpalatable    →   the Natal
to predators              grass cycad
```

When correct answers are conditional, they're usually written in contrapositive form (to be sneaky, to disguise their potential appeal). When we contrapose this one, we get:

```
can't feed on the        no means to make
Natal grass cycad    →   itself highly yucky

```

Did the author's argument make that move?

He must be thinking that without this plant, the moth loses this defense mechanism, and thus the predators will be able to gobble them up to the point where their species will be in danger of surviving.

item: PT150-S2-Q12: in the D note, a hypothetical is labeled "(A)"

For example, if an answer said,

We'd immediately eliminate it. The conclusion is supposed to be on the right side (the outcome) of a conditional reasoning move.

We want to see
premise → conclusion

However, when you contrapose that reasoning move (as so many correct answers do), you get:
not conclusion → not premise

So seeing the negation of the conclusion in the trigger is a great sign. That's what we're seeing here. The answer says,

```
someone afraid of sci's       scientists
```

item: PT149-S1-Q10: author disowns the question ("hot garbage", "ignore this question ever existed")
old:
This answer is supposed to be communicating, "these black and white species really DO have effective camouflage! Even though their coloration seems (to human perception) to be unlikely to provide effective camouflage, to many animals species, their perception of color and pattern might be such that to them this black and white coloration is effective camouflage."

Where do I begin with my problems with this answer choice?
- when I read in an LSAT paragraph that these species have coloration that seems unlikely to provide effective camouflage, I am assuming that this is a FACT coming from a source that is informed about the animal kingdom, not an uninformed opinion by someone who just looks at black and white and says "I reckon that wouldn't be good camouflage".

- it seems like a high percentage of us (maybe even a majority) already know what (C) is saying. It doesn't provide any new information, because it is already thoroughly within normal common sense that there are differences in how animals of different species perceive color and pattern.

- the intended logical force of this answer is only very weakly suggested by the actual language of the answer. There's a big gap between "many animals perceive color/pattern differently from how humans do" and "these animals find this black and white coloration difficult to discern".

My recommendation for all of us is to ignore this question ever existed. There is nothing to learn here except the humility that comes with knowing that the test writers sometimes just write terrible questions that we can't blame ourselves for not finding our way through.
new:
This answer is communicating, "these black and white species really DO have effective camouflage! Even though their coloration seems (to human perception) to be unlikely to provide effective camouflage, to many animal species, their perception of color and pattern might be such that to them this black and white coloration is effective camouflage."

The paradox only works if the coloration really fails as camouflage. But the stimulus never says it fails. It says the coloration "seems unlikely" to work, and that judgment comes from how the coloration looks to us.

If many predators do not perceive color or pattern the way humans do, then a pattern that looks conspicuous to us may be hard for those predators to pick out. That would explain how prey with few other defenses have endured for a long time.

(C) doesn't prove that this particular coloration works against these particular predators, but it gives us a plausible way for the coloration to protect the prey, and that is all a resolve answer needs to do. item: PT143-S1-Q19: worked example moves from OKC to "Austin" mid-sentence
old:
This is a tricky mathematical paradox. If the average wage went up in each region, then how could the average wage go down nationally?
Normally, we don't spend too much time up front on Paradox questions trying to guess the answer because there could potentially be a lot of ways to resolve the Paradox. But when it's mathematical, there is often only one way.
In this case, in order for every region's average to go up while the national average went down, we need there to be a net effect of people moving out of regions whose average is higher than the national average into areas whose average is lower than the national average.
Say that the average wage nationally is $25 / hr. Some regions, like San Francisco, will have regional average wage of $30 / hr. Some regions like, like Oklahoma City, will have a regional average wage of $20 / hr.
Let's say, last year, OKC's average rose to $21 / hr and SF's average rose to $31 / hr.
We'd expect the national average to start creeping towards $26 / hr. But now consider the effect if tons of people move from SF to OKC.
Someone who used to be making $30 / hr in SF now lives in Austin and makes $21 / hr.
When it comes to the national average hourly wage, people who made $30 / hr last year but make $21 / hr this year are going to bring that average down.
Or in case this makes more sense, suppose that SF is a region with a $30 / hr average wage. OKC is a region with a $20 / hr average wage. Bob lives in SF and makes $28 / hr.
Now he moves to OKC and makes $25 / hr. What has he done to the average wage in SF, OKC, and nationally?
He raised the average wage in SF, because if the average is 30 and you get rid of a data point that is 28, then that will boost the average. (If you kick a teenager off your team, then the average age of your team will go up).
He raised the average wage in OKC, because the average there was $20, but he makes $25. And he lowered the national average, because he went from making $28 to $25.

item: PT143-S3-Q5: A note says "The town is not an economic wasteland"; the sense needs "now"
old:
A lot of times on Paradox questions, to break out of the paradox's confusion and into the enlightenment of the answer, we have to do a gestalt shift (think about it a very different way).

Our paradox was:
If there's a high level of unemployment, then people don't have jobs, so they don't have money, so they shouldn't be able to afford a house. How is it that these communities have high levels of home ownership?

But that's because we're thinking
1st came the unemployed
2nd came buying the house

If we reverse that chronology, then this answer can help us make sense of things.

1st came buying the house (the people in town had jobs at that point). Let's say we're in West Virginia during the glory days of coal mining. People had jobs, so they had money, so they bought homes, so there is a really high rate of home ownership.

But then .... coal mines get shut down. Most of the good local jobs disappear. The town is not an economic wasteland.

The people who rent month-to-month have the freedom to pack up and say, "I'm moving to a different area with better job opportunities".

The people who are stuck in 30 year mortgages can't just uproot like that. They have to stay and stick it out in an economically depressed area.

So high levels of home ownership go hand-in-hand with high levels of unemployment because, "the only reason you'd stay in an area with high levels of unemployment is if you were stuck living there because you bought a home and planted your roots".

item: PT126-S4-Q5: conditional diagram lost its line break ("needed drugsdidn't receive drugs")
old:
This correct answer is pretty miserable. It's one of those ones where if you weren't already thinking what LSAT wanted you to be thinking, then you wouldn't see anything in this answer to provoke that thinking in you.

This is getting at the idea that medical specialists only give physical therapy to patients who can recover with physical therapy alone, whereas they give physical therapy and drugs to patients who would need both in order to recover.

So the drugs are a necessary part of the treatment for those who receive it, because the medical specialist accurately judged that those people needed drugs.

And drugs were not necessary to those who didn't receive them. If you wanted to, you could put this into conditional form:

received drugs → needed drugsdidn't receive drugs → didn't need drugs

Even though the patients w/o drugs recovered as much as the patients w/ drugs, the drugs were still necessary for those who got them, because the medical specialist made an accurate judgment in assessing whether that patient needed drugs.

If it sounds a little circular, it almost is, but it's really just getting at the simpler real-world idea that a specialist will prescribe physical therapy for milder cases of back injuries and physical therapy + drugs for more severe cases.

If she succeeds in getting all her patients to recover, it might look like drugs did nothing, but it could otherwise be that drugs did do something, and she was wise/accurate enough to only give it to the people who actually needed the drugs.

In real life, smart tech people like Elon Musk make arguments similar to this to argue that we probably live in a simulation: if there were simulated universes, there would be way more simulated universes than real universes, so the probability would be much higher that you live in a simulated universe than in the real universe. Thus, you probably live in a simulated universe. On Method, our job is just to characterize the type of evidence used or the type of move the author made, and the correct answer usually sounds like one of these options: analogy, rule out alternatives, implications of logic, example / counterexample, definition / distinction, overlooked consideration, dubious assumption, alternative explanation The key moment that would stick out to me in this argument is the moment of "Suppose they're right ...." / "If that were really so ... " This is what we mean when we say "implications of logic". The second half of an If/Then statement is called its outcome, its consequence, its necessary implication. So authors will either say, "Let's follow the logic of your plan or your rule ... it ultimately ends at this undesirable place, so it looks like the plan / rule is no good". Or, like we're doing in this argument, authors will say, "If you were right, then X would follow. But X isn't true. So you must be wrong." This 2nd style is arguing via contrapositive logic. If you were right → implication X But implication X is not the case. Thus, you are not right.

item: PT138-S3-Q20: "real crappy argument", "This correct answer is miserable", and an Elon Musk aside
old:
Any time an answer is structured
infers that since X, Y
we would see the X part as referring to the evidence and the Y part as referring to the conclusion.
Is the conclusion saying "a hypothesis is probably false"?
It's saying that "the belief that the galaxy will eventually be colonized by trillions of humans" is probably false. It's a little weird to call that a hypothesis, which is normally used to mean "a claim that posits an explanation for a phenomenon".
This is more using "hypothesis" to mean "speculative guess", which is normal in real life but very uncommon in LSAT. What makes it more like a hypothesis than just a mere prediction, I suppose, is that the first sentence is saying, "Given that humans tend to explore and colonize new areas, people hypothesize that will one day colonize and inhabit the galaxy".
Okay, we've begrudgingly signed off on the conclusion part. Was the evidence saying that "an event is taken to be likely on a given hypothesis"?
Yes, that's saying "given the truth of this hypothesis, event X would be likely", and our evidence was saying,
"were the hypothesis that humans colonized the galaxy true, it is likely (the odds are overwhelming) that we would be living during this time period".
Can we call that an event? Yeesh, I'd rather not. This correct answer is miserable.
Can we say that event has not occurred? Yes, the author says "we are not alive during this period", so the 'event' of us living during the time of galactic colonization has not occurred.
If we were to put this answer in more apt terms, it's saying that the author is
"concluding that, since a likely implication of a given prediction is not the case, the prediction will probably not occur."
This is definitely a great example of the ol' mantra:
We have to pick the best-available answer, even if it's not quite an acceptable answer.
I think hypothesis and event are both really curiously bad terms for this conversation.

item: PT106-S1-Q7: E note says "mental disorders"; the stimulus is about neurological disorders
old:
Yikes, this is a tough answer to match up.

The key phrase is that the money should be "used to minimize patients' suffering".

The auditor's argument is assuming that this phrase means that "using money to minimize patients' suffering = letting that money flow directly to patients".

Meanwhile, the administrator is arguing that we don't have to interpret "using money to minimize patients' suffering" in that direct sense.

We would still be spending money to minimize patients' suffering indirectly, in the long run, by funding research that we hope will lead to earlier detection of mental disorders.

Put another way, the auditor is assuming that "minimize patients' suffering" should be interpreted as "find existing patients who are suffering, and reduce that suffering".

The administrator is seeking to interpret "minimize patients' suffering" as being compatible with "do things to prevent suffering from happening in the first place".

item: PT148-S3-Q26: Evaluate flips a sign; algebra table flattened
old:
Since we're seeing *conditional logic* (if)*, quantifiers* (most), a *volume dial* (the more x, the more y), and *repeating ideas* (new/old, ruled by monarch), it seems like we should turn this argument into abstract algebra.

We have two premises:

P1: Most countries are not *Most C's are ~M*
ruled by monarchs

P2: The older a country, *The more O,*
the more likely it's *the more likely M*
ruled by a monarch

C: If a country is new, *If ~O,*
it's probably not ruled *then prob ~M*
by a monarch

This argument's logic is pretty sound. Say there are 100 countries. We know at most 49 of them are ruled by monarchs.

From that claim, we could say "If it's a country, then it's probably not ruled by a monarch", but we wouldn't be able to say "if it's a *new* country, then it's probably not ruled by a monarch."

Why? Because the *new* countries might be atypical. It might be that all the new countries are ruled by monarchs, but only 30% of countries are new. If all the other countries are **not** ruled by monarchs, then it would be true that "most countries are not ruled by monarchs", but it *wouldn't* be true that "if a country is new, it's probably ruled by a monarch".

But, the other premise removes this possibility. It's impossible for the new ones to be the ones ruled by monarchs and the older ones to be the ones not ruled by monarchs when we add the premise that "the older the country, the more likely it's ruled by a monarch".

P1: Most countries are not ruled by monarchs.
*Most C's are ~M*

P2: The older a country, the more likely it's ruled by a monarch.
*The more O, the more likely M*

C: If a country is new, it's probably not ruled by a monarch.
*If ~O, then prob ~M*

This argument's logic is pretty sound. Say there are 100 countries. We know at most 49 of them are ruled by monarchs.

From that claim, we could say "If it's a country, then it's probably not ruled by a monarch", but we wouldn't be able to say "if it's a *new* country, then it's probably not ruled by a monarch."

Why? Because the *new* countries might be atypical. It might be that all the new countries are ruled by monarchs, but only 30% of countries are new. If all the other countries are **not** ruled by monarchs, then it would be true that "most countries are not ruled by monarchs", but it *wouldn't* be true that "if a country is new, it's probably not ruled by a monarch".

But, the other premise removes this possibility. It's impossible for the new ones to be the ones ruled by monarchs and the older ones to be the ones not ruled by monarchs when we add the premise that "the older the country, the more likely it's ruled by a monarch".
why: The two-column algebra table was flattened so the English and the symbols interleaved; and the counter-scenario (all new countries ruled by monarchs) falsifies 'new means probably NOT ruled by a monarch', so the dropped 'not' is restored.
evidence: Conclusion: 'if a country is particularly new it is probably not ruled by a monarch.' Evaluate: 'It might be that all the new countries are ruled by monarchs'.

After reading the argument on a Parallel question, we have to decide whether we think it would be more effective to make an Algebra Recipe for the argument or to just boil it down to a Principle or Reasoning Pattern. My general rule of thumb is that if there's conditional logic or quantifiers or Overlapping Ideas, then I'll go for Algebra. The first two premises are quantified/conditional logic (no / every). And there are Overlapping Ideas: Carriage Books, nonfiction book, profit, publish are all mentioned at least twice. So if we assign them some variables, we can look at the logic.
```
Premise 1 — No X's from Thing A have ever been Y.
  For Thing A (all time): if X → no Y
Premise 2 — Every Z from Thing A's last year was Y.
  For Thing A (last year): if Z → yes Y
Conclusion — Thing A last year didn't have any Z's that were X
  For Thing A (last year): if Z → not X
```
Since Carriage Books is the common ingredient to all three claims, I would focus more on the movings parts.
```
Nonfiction is never profitable.   N → ~P
Last yr's books were profitable.  Last yr = P
So, last yr's books were fiction. Last yr = ~N
```

item: PT138-S2-Q25 (golden): Evaluate says the "only if" term goes on the right side "(sufficient condition)"
old: Since this has three conditional logic claims (if / only if / if) and has ideas that show up multiple times (squirrels eat / attract birds / protective cover), we would probably be wise to diagram this symbolically. And since we're doing Flaw / Parallel Flaw and we're seeing conditional logic, we can already be 90% sure that the flaw in the argument is an illegal negation or reversal (i.e. the Necessary vs. Sufficient flaw). The author is trying to put together two conditionals to arrive at her conclusion. Since "squirrels eating" is the common term in the two conditional premises, it's supposed to be the middle link in the chain. The author thinks she's combining these two premises: No cover → Squirrels eat Squirrels eat → Not many birds If those were actually the two premises, then she would correctly be deriving her conclusion: No cover -—--—--—--—> Not many birds The problem is the second premise says, Squirrels eat → No cover The word "only if" is the opposite of "if". When we see "if", the idea that goes with that word ends up on the left side of the arrow (the sufficient condition). When we see "only if", the idea that goes with that ends up on the right side (sufficient condition).

item: Side 1: PT108-S3-Q6 (answer-placement rule in Evaluate)
label: Evaluate
old:
This isn't a true paradox. Nothing here is surprising. The stem just wants explanations for a drop in the number of bass caught.

Think about what "number of bass caught" depends on. It takes two things: bass in the water and people fishing for them. So there are two roads to fewer bass caught:
1. **Fewer bass downstream.** They died, got eaten, moved away, or lost their habitat.
2. **Less fishing downstream.** Fewer anglers, or anglers fishing less.

Usually, on EXCEPT questions, three of the four answers we eliminate come at the stimulus from one angle, and the fourth takes a different tactic. Here, expect three answers on road 1 and one sneaking in on road 2.

Most students only think of road 1, because the wastewater feels like it must be hurting the fish. But road 2 is just as good. If half the anglers stop showing up, half as many bass get caught, even if the bass are thriving.
new:
This isn't a true paradox. Nothing here is surprising. The stem just wants explanations for a drop in the number of bass caught.

Think about what "number of bass caught" depends on. It takes two things: bass in the water and people fishing for them. So there are two roads to fewer bass caught:
1. **Fewer bass downstream.** They died, got eaten, moved away, or lost their habitat.
2. **Less fishing downstream.** Fewer anglers, or anglers fishing less.

Expect most of the answers we eliminate to come in on road 1, with at least one sneaking in on road 2.

Most students only think of road 1, because the wastewater feels like it must be hurting the fish. But road 2 is just as good. If half the anglers stop showing up, half as many bass get caught, even if the bass are thriving.
why: Removes a claim about how EXCEPT answer sets are usually built; keeps the two-road teaching point.
evidence: Choices A, B, E work on road 1 (fewer bass); D works on road 2 (fewer anglers).

This paragraph doesn't read too much as an *argument*, but the first sentence *is* an opinion ("superior"). Our usual goal when we're matching a Principle to an argument is to make the conclusion be the outcome of the principle, and a consideration from the evidence to be the trigger of the principle.
  If the conclusion is saying "one system is superior to another", then we want a principle that helps us judge the *superiority* of a theory.
  Why does our author think C's theory was better than P's theory?
  P posited something that C found unlikely. And C ** thought of a simpler theory.
  We obviously know that C's theory is borne out as the correct one, but why did the author find it superior *at the time it was proposed*, even though the available evidence was equally consistent with both theories?
  The superiority must have been its simplicity. That's the famous principle known as Ockham's Razor (the literal phrasing is something like "avoid superfluous entities", but the usage is that "all other things being equal, the simpler explanation is the better one").

item: Side 5: spaces lost around bold/italic (PT106-S3-Q24 'aCurious')
label: Evaluate
old:
The author is thinking purely in terms of numbers.
She thinks that during the 17th century, major artists would have produced way fewer Dutch landscapes than minor artists would have (since minor artists were cranking these out prolifically, trying to satisfy the insatiable demands of the market).
So let's say for example that major artists created 100 of these paintings, whereas minor artists created 1000 of them.
The author is thinking, "if the surviving paintings are supposedly 1/2 major, 1/2 minor that's gotta be wrong. After all, the ratio of major to minor wasn't 1:1, it was more like 1 : 10."
We could call this aCurious Comparison-- how could it be that major artists made less than half of the Dutch landscapes in the 17th century but are attributed to half of the surviving ones?
The author's way of explaining this is, "We must be misattributing a bunch of these ones done by minor artists to major artists".
We, of course, are tasked with considering Alternate Explanations .... "Maybe a Dutch landscape painted by amajorartist would be much more likely to survive for several centuries than would one painted by a minor artist."
After all, the ones painted by major artists would be more valuable, presumably, so people would have more incentive to hang onto them. And perhaps they were owned by wealthier people, whose belongings and estates have been better preserved and attended to.
The Dutch landscapes painted by minor artists to satisfy rabid public demand might have been cheap to purchase, painted on cheaper (more degrading) materials, and thus many more of them would have ended up in the garbage eventually.

item: PT158-S3-Q13 E argues against "will not help patients address any difficulties they have in their relationships"
old: This answer discusses what happens when a therapist focuses on "purely internal" troubles, but the argument's conclusion is about what the therapist must focus on (relationships), not about the consequences of focusing on the wrong thing. Additionally, the claim that focusing on internal troubles "will not help patients address any difficulties they have in their relationships" is a claim about consequences for relationships, while the argument's conclusion is about healing the patient — healing and improving relationships are related but not identical goals. The argument needs the assumption that internal-only treatment cannot achieve healing, not a specific claim about whether internal-focused therapy affects relationships. This answer addresses a tangential consequence rather than the core logical link between evidence and conclusion.
new: This answer is about what happens when a therapist helps patients focus on "troubles that are purely internal": it says that focus "thereby provides them the relief they seek." That is a claim about when internal-only therapy succeeds, and the argument does not need it. If anything, it points the other way, since the psychotherapist says the troubles "do not have purely internal causes" and that the therapist must focus on relationships. The argument needs the assumption that internal-only treatment cannot achieve healing. Negate this answer, "focusing on purely internal troubles does not provide the relief they seek," and the argument is untouched.
why: The note argued against a choice about internal focus not helping relationships, which is not E; E says internal focus provides relief, which the argument does not require and its negation leaves intact.
evidence: E: 'If a psychotherapist helps patients focus on troubles that are purely internal, then that psychotherapist thereby provides them the relief they seek.'

item: PT158-S3-Q17 A-D notes describe choices that do not exist ("(2) enjoy learning math", etc.)
old: The teacher wants students to (1) understand mathematical principles and (2) enjoy learning math. The analysis pattern applies: if students understand the principles being taught (objective 1), they will naturally enjoy the learning experience more (objective 2). Understanding creates engagement, which creates enjoyment. This mirrors the original: achieving a cognitive/experiential improvement (understanding/enjoyment) leads to a behavioral outcome (enjoyment/more time). The causal link between comprehension and enjoyment is a standard motivational connection — people tend to enjoy activities they understand and can succeed at. This fits the pattern.
new: The teacher wants students to (1) understand the mathematical principles taught in the course and (2) apply these principles routinely in everyday life. The analysis pattern applies: if students truly understand the principles (objective 1), they are better able, and more likely, to use them outside class (objective 2). You cannot routinely apply what you do not understand. This mirrors the original, where achieving the first goal (enjoying the challenge) brings about the second (more time practicing). This fits the pattern.
why: The note invented a second objective ('enjoy learning math'); A's second objective is applying the principles routinely in everyday life, and understanding plausibly brings that about.
evidence: A: 'A math teacher wants her students to understand the mathematical principles taught in her course and wants them to apply these principles routinely in everyday life.'

item: PT158-S3-Q17 A-D notes describe choices that do not exist ("(2) enjoy learning math", etc.)
old: The software manufacturer wants customers to (1) be more satisfied with its product and (2) have customers recommend the product to others. The analysis pattern applies: if customers are more satisfied (objective 1), they will naturally recommend the product to others (objective 2). Satisfied customers become advocates — this is the core logic of word-of-mouth marketing. The causal link is direct and intuitive: positive experience leads to positive recommendation. This perfectly mirrors the original's pattern where an internal state improvement (satisfaction/enjoyment) leads to a desired behavioral outcome (recommendations/more practice time).
new: The software manufacturer wants customers to (1) be more satisfied with its product and (2) place fewer calls to the service representative about how to use the product. The analysis pattern applies: if customers are more satisfied with the product (objective 1), that plausibly includes finding it easier to use, so they call less often for help using it (objective 2). This mirrors the original's pattern, where an improvement in how people experience something (satisfaction/enjoyment) brings about the desired behavior (fewer help calls/more practice time).
why: The note invented a second objective ('recommend the product'); B's second objective is fewer calls to the service representative about how to use the product, which more satisfied customers plausibly make.
evidence: B: 'A software manufacturer wants its customers to be more satisfied with its product, and it wants them to place fewer calls to the service representative about how to use the product.'

item: PT158-S3-Q17 A-D notes describe choices that do not exist ("(2) enjoy learning math", etc.)
old: The librarian wants (1) fewer borrowed books to be lost or stolen and (2) borrowers to return books in good condition. The analysis pattern applies: if fewer books are lost or stolen (objective 1), borrowers are treating books more responsibly overall, which means they will also return books in better condition (objective 2). Both objectives are symptoms of the same underlying behavior — responsible handling of borrowed materials. Fostering the care that prevents loss and theft (objective 1) naturally extends to the care that preserves book condition (objective 2). item: PT112-S1-Q9 B "close to being 3 mg iron per capita" (per calorie)
old:
This is offering us a story of how a grape sheds calories en route to being a raisin.

The grape had 20mg of iron and 10 calories. **2 mg iron per calorie**

The raisin keeps that 20mg of iron. "The only thing removed from the grapes is water".

But the sugar in the grape caramelizes as it becomes a raisin. And when we measure how many calories something has, we don't count calories in caramelized sugar (because the body can't digest it).

So when we measure the raisin that formed from that 10 calorie grape, we get a number lower than 10.

Some of the grape's 10 calories were from sugar. When that sugar caramelized, then those sugar-calories stop being counted.

If there were 3 calories from the sugar, then now that the grape has caramelized into a raisin, that 10 calorie grape will only be a 7 calorie raisin.

And if the raisin has 20mg of iron and is only 7 calories, then it's close to being **3 mg iron per capita**.

So this answer allows us to explain why a raisin made from a given grape can have more iron per calorie than the grape, even though no iron is added and only water is removed.
